name: Leek hair dye

lead: Leek hair dye refers to ancient preparations made from leeks, recorded in Roman sources as a way to darken or recolour hair. Its appearance payoff was masking grey and achieving the fashionable darker shade.
Accounts describe a decoction of the leek outer coat, and encyclopedia entries describe a black dye of leeks and boiled walnuts. No modern studies have tested it.

paras: Historically, leek parts were boiled and the liquid applied to hair. Modern use is rare and mostly of historical interest.
No modern safety data exists. Plant dyes can cause skin allergy in some people, and the practice is not a regulated cosmetic product.

angle.text: In ancient Rome, leek-based preparations were used to darken grey hair. Sources describe the effect qualitatively; no measured results exist.

lead: Leek hair dye is an ancient Roman plant-based hair colouring. A passage in Pliny the Elder's Natural History, as reported in secondary sources, describes a decoction of the outer coat of the leek acting as a dye on grey hair.[1]

Roman hair fashion ran from blond, popular and associated with Gaul and Germany, to red and black, and many Romans reportedly preferred a black dye of leeks and boiled walnuts.[2] The appeal of such dyes was disguising grey and changing colour using kitchen and garden plants.
Leeks are listed among ancient plant-derived hair dyes alongside henna, indigo and walnut hulls.[3] No published modern trial has examined leek preparations as a hair colourant.

paras: Plant-based hair dyes date back millennia; examples include Egyptian recipes in the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) and Assyrian recipes.[3] Roman fashion favoured blond, red and black shades, with gold dust available to the very wealthy.[2] Leek preparations belong to the dark-dye tradition: a decoction of the leek outer coat for grey hair, and a leek-and-walnut black dye.[2][1]

timeline.event: Ebers Papyrus records dye recipes for grey hair.[3]
Pliny the Elder's Natural History mentions a leek decoction as a dye for grey hair.[1]
